newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria beefs up controls against oil smugglers.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria beefs up controls against oil smugglers.

text.p: Bulgaria, heavily hit by fuel shortages, plans to privatise part of its troubled Neftochim refinery, raise fuel prices and stiffen border controls to cope with a crippling fuel shortage, the interim prime minister said.

"Neftochim will be privatised partially," Stefan Sofianski told reporters. He gave no details about his plans for the refinery, which supplies almost the whole of the domestic market but recently ran out of cash to pay for crude oil supplies.
"A drastic hike of fuel prices is urgent and the interim cabinet will discuss it on Monday," Stefan Sofianski told reporters.
He earlier said he would ban fuel exports although this would not affect the contracted volumes by the country's biggest oil refinery Neftochim.
"From today we ban any fuel exports and if necessary we will have troops on borders but we must stop speculations with fuel," Sofianski said.

Local media say motorists smuggle cans full of petrol of diesel to neighbouring Yugoslavia and Macedonia, where prices are higher. Fuel shortages are threatening to paralyse Bulgaria because the country does not have cash to pay for crude supplies.

Most petrol stations in the country have been closed because of the fuel shortage and municipalities are distributing petrol and diesel for ambulances, food delivery trucks, the police, the army and other social services, officials said.
Production has been hit by cuts in bus services, transport officials said.

Neftochim, which supplies almost the whole domestic market, has debts worth millions of dollars because of low domestic prices and suppliers have refused to deliver crude to the cash-stripped refinery.

Refinery officials say regular government revisions of fuel prices have not kept up with a recent drastic fall of the lev against the dollar. A litre of gasoline now costs 10 cents, as the price has been based on a rate of 660 levs per dollar.
The Bulgarian lev traded 3,020-3,050 per dollar on Friday.
"We will take steps by Sunday for opening new credit lines for Neftohim and for rescheduling the plant's debts to the banks," Sofianski said.
Sofianski, who visited Neftochimin the Black Sea port of Bourgas late on Thursday, said the interim government would seek financial stabilisation of the plant.

Earlier this week Neftochim agreed a $50-million credit with France's Paribas Bank branch in Geneva after Russia's state-owned Rosneft oil company guaranteed half of the credit line. Rosneft holds a 50-pecent stake in a joint venture with Neftochim.
Sofianski said the government had stiffened border controls on Friday in an attempt to curb fuel smuggling.
The interim cabinet on Thursday sacked the board of directors of Neftochim. The board is due to submit a stabilisation programme in the next two weeks.

The refinery is distributing limited volumes of 680 tonnes of petrol and 680 tonnes of diesel per day. It has been refining 8,500 tonnes of crude per day since Tuesday, while its daily capacity is 25,000.
A 66,300-tonne tanker from Russia's Rosbulneft arrived on Wednesday at Bourgas port under its February contract for crude deliveries to Neftochim.
